title: The Value Belief
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: In this guide to the Value belief, the second of Dave Stuart Jr.'s Five Key Beliefs of student motivation, Stuart argues that American secondary classrooms lean far too heavily on just two motivational levers, utility and relevance, and that this narrowness quietly damages students' hearts. He introduces the Rainbow of Why, a nine-color spectrum of reasons students might value schoolwork, urging teachers to paint with all of them rather than defaulting to you'll use this someday. Drawing on research from Bryan et al. and a Purdie-and-Hattie study on students' conceptions of learning, he shows that breadth of framing, not any single correct philosophy of learning, predicts achievement. He then narrows the strategy set to three core moves, Mini-Sermons, Feast of Knowledge, and Valued Within Exercises, and closes with practical answers to common hang-ups about competition, grade-mongering, and students from homes where education isn't valued.
points: Stuart names two motivational defaults, utility and relevance, as overused and psychologically weak, citing research that people discount the value of temporally distant rewards to an extreme and irrational degree.

The Rainbow of Why reframes Value as a nine-color spectrum (utility, relevance, social status, autonomy, justice/prosocial, novelty, enjoyment, meaning/purpose, beauty) teachers can intentionally rotate through rather than relying on one or two colors.
Purdie and Hattie's research found no single correct conception of learning predicts achievement; instead, students who hold more conceptions of learning simultaneously tend to do better in school.
His grading philosophy for reducing grade-mongering keeps the gradebook simple, using sparse formative entries and test corrections while relentlessly repeating that the goal is mastery, not grades.
quotes: For a human to be optimally motivated in an endeavor, they need a core question answered: does this work actually matter? Unfortunately, the average secondary student answers this with a simple "no.
First, they don't work all that well, especially when we make utility arguments about the future: People discount the value of temporally distant rewards to an extreme and irrational degree.
The biggest problem I see in teachers who rely too much on relevance is that they presume that student interests are more homogenous than they actually are.
My point is to critique the popular narrative amongst American educators that relevant curricula are a simple and self-evident good.

The more conceptions they had, the better they tended to do in school. I don't know why that is, but my guess is that a student with such a broad array of outlooks has an easier time engaging with any learning task they're presented with.
The main thing that I find helps is that I keep my grading system as simple as possible.
Overall, the most powerful thing we can do to help students who are obsessed with grades is speak to the truth that our goal is mastery, not grades.
